title: Opening Range Breakout
teaches: The opening range breakout as we trade it: an entry timer on 30-minute bars for a daily setup already on the focus list (a Kicker, an earnings gap, a base breakout) in a leader above its 50-day and 200-day; the range is the first 30-minute candle, 9:30 to 10:00 ET; the buy is the trade a cent through its high after 10:00 at market, never more than 4% past it; the stop sits a few cents under the day's low at the fill; the first sell is a judgment, usually day 3 or later into a 3, 5 or 7 day push, with the rest on the trail; on a Kicker the stop is capped at 3.5%; a loss at the stop is the plan working.

facts.quote: In this book I define the Opening Range as the first 30 minutes of the trading day.
facts.claim: Bysshe defines the opening range as the first 30 minutes of the day.

facts.quote: the 30-minute OR is defined as the stock's high and low for the day at 10:00 AM. The OR is not the opening price.
facts.claim: Bysshe: the 30-minute range is the day's high and low at 10:00, not the opening print.

facts.quote: If the OR is sloppy, that is, if there isn't any well-defined support or resistance, don't waste your time watching it.
facts.claim: Bysshe skips a sloppy range with no well-defined high or low.

facts.quote: The daily trend should be positive. Both the 20-day and the 50-day moving averages are positively sloped and the stock is trading above the 20-day moving average.
facts.claim: Bysshe wants a positive daily trend: rising 20 and 50-day averages, price above the 20-day.

facts.quote: A bullish bias pattern in the OR may give you a hint, but your best clue is volume.
facts.claim: Bysshe: the best clue in the opening range is volume.

facts.quote: a period of time equal to half the time period of the OR.
facts.claim: Bysshe's clean-break rule of thumb: after the break, price holds above the range for a period equal to half the range's own length, which is 15 minutes on a 30-minute range.

facts.quote: your maximum risk point for an OR breakout is the low of the OR.
facts.claim: Bysshe's widest stop on a range break is the range low.

facts.quote: If I can't find a good stop or risk point then I generally pass on the trade.
facts.claim: Bysshe passes when no good stop can be found.

facts.quote: First identify a list of candidates based on your swing trade criteria, and then use the OR to time your entry.
facts.claim: Bysshe: pick the swing candidates first, then use the opening range to time the entry.

facts.quote: The result is you buy a stock that has already moved too far from your optimal entry point.
facts.claim: Bysshe on chasing a strong open: you buy too far from the right entry.

facts.quote: Enter on the opening range highs.
facts.claim: Kullamagi enters a breakout at the opening range high.

facts.quote: The opening range highs can be the highs of the first 1-minute candle, the 5-minute candle or the 60-minute candle (on the 60-minute timeframe the first candle is always only 30 minutes, 9.30-10 AM).
facts.claim: Kullamagi: on a 60-minute chart the first candle is only 30 minutes, 9:30 to 10:00.

facts.quote: Stop is always lows of the day and stop should not be wider than the ATR or ADR of the stock
facts.claim: Kullamagi: the stop is the low of the day, no wider than the stock's ATR or ADR.

facts.quote: Many times the best ones have traded their average daily volume in the first 15-30 minutes after the open.
facts.claim: Kullamagi: the best gap plays trade their average daily volume in the first 15 to 30 minutes.

facts.quote: You should sell 1/3 to 1/2 of the position after 3-5 days, and then move the stop to break even.
facts.claim: Kullamagi sells a third to a half after 3 to 5 days, then moves the stop to breakeven.

facts.quote: You don’t even have to use any intraday chart, just look at the daily chart and enter when the stock is starting to break out.
facts.claim: Kullamagi: the setup is on the daily chart; the intraday chart only times the entry.

facts.quote: The 30-minute opening range is the high and low of the first 30 minute candle of the day. An opening range breakout is the first time price trades above that high.
facts.claim: Trade-Ideas: the 30-minute range is the first 30-minute candle's high and low; the breakout is the first trade above that high.

facts.quote: The morning range is defined by the high and low made in the first 45-120 minutes. Different time parameters can be used, but the most popular one is the first hour's range.
facts.claim: Raschke's morning range is longer, 45 to 120 minutes; windows differ by trader.

facts.quote: The good news is that breakout strategies have a high win/loss ratio. The bad news is that whipsaws can be brutal!
facts.claim: Raschke: breakout strategies win often, and the whipsaws are brutal.

facts.quote: An opening range breakout (ORB) is a trade taken at a predetermined amount above or below the opening range.
facts.claim: Crabel's definition: a trade taken a set amount beyond the opening range.

facts.quote: My hypothesis is that inside days precede trend day activity and, consequently, successful opening range breakouts.

facts.quote: This makes the first pullback after the breakout move a nice high-probability entry once you start to see resumed buying.

walkthroughs.title: FFIV, September 2026: the cleanest break
steps: FFIV, September 15, 2026. A leader with RS 81, over its 50-day and 200-day. It opens flat on 2.67 times normal volume.
At 10:00 the first 30-minute candle sets the range: 418.45 high, 412.06 low. That high's already above yesterday's high.
The very next candle trades a cent through 418.45. Buy at market, 418.46. Stop 412.01, a few cents under the low.
A heavy-volume reversal back into the range would be your warning. It never looked back. 3R in two sessions.

walkthroughs.title: SNX, September 2026: the trims and the gap
steps: September 21, 2026: SNX gaps 2.3% over yesterday's high. At 10:05 it clears the 274.03 range high: buy 274.04, stop 270.67.
Check the calendar: earnings were September 24, 3 sessions out. We don't buy that close to a report.
It hit 5R in two sessions anyway. Sell some into the push and move the stop to breakeven.
September 24 the report gaps it through the stop. The first 30-minute low becomes the stop. What you sold kept the win.

walkthroughs.title: JBI, December 2023: the Kicker's two entries
steps: JBI, December 14, 2023, a Kicker day. It opens under the red day's high, so you've got two entries in play.
First one: it trades through that high inside the first 30 minutes. Fill 11.05, stop 10.80, 2.3% away.
Second one: the ORB, a cent over the first 30-minute high, fills at 11.21. Same stop is now 3.7% away.
That's past our 3.5% Kicker cap, so the stop comes up to 10.82. At the close: first fill 2.3R, the ORB 1.0R.

questions.q: It's 10:00 and you're marking the opening range on your 30-minute chart. What exactly are you marking?
questions.why: The high and low from 9:30 to 10:00, the first 30-minute candle. That's the window we use. The opening print is one trade. You want the whole first half hour, the high the buyers made and the low the sellers made. Mark both at 10:00. The high is your trigger. Your stop will sit a few cents under the low. A strong mover can still be bought right at the open when it triggers properly, but that's a different plan.
questions.lesson_line: Mark the first half hour's high and low at 10:00. That's your range.

wrong.The first 5-minute bar: That's the opening drive's bar, a faster trade with its own rules. The ORB waits for the full half hour.
wrong.The opening print: One print tells you nothing. The range is the high and low the first half hour actually made.
wrong.The 9:30 to 10:30 high and low: That's a full hour. Some traders use longer windows, but our range closes at 10:00.

questions.simple: Mark the high and low of the first half hour, 9:30 to 10:00. The high is your trigger.

deeper.counter: Windows differ across traders. Raschke's morning range runs 45 to 120 minutes, most popularly the first hour. Kullamagi uses the first 1-minute, 5-minute or 60-minute candle. Bysshe and Trade-Ideas use the first 30 minutes, as we do. So the range we mark is 9:30 to 10:00.

reasons: rests on the house 30-minute window (D-031 pending; 30 minutes kept as the default in every option)

questions.q: The ORB trigger is the first trade through the 30-minute high, not a candle closing above it.
questions.why: True. You don't wait for a close. The moment price trades through the high after 10:00, that's your buy, at market. Waiting for a candle to finish just gets you a higher fill. On the strong ones it gets you no fill at all, because it's already gone. Set an alert at the range high the minute the range is in, so you're ready when it trades.
questions.lesson_line: When it trades through the high, you trade.
questions.simple: True, we buy the moment price trades through the high. We don't wait for a candle to close.

reasons: fixed before (the lesson line was corrected on 2026-11-10)

questions.q: Where's your stop?
questions.why: A few cents under 143.91, the low of the day. Here that's 143.86. The low is where the chart says you're wrong. If buyers can't hold the day's low, the break failed. Put the stop right on the low and a wick that just tests it takes you out. So it goes a few cents under. From your fill that's 2.07%, right inside the 1 to 3% I like. This was ANF. Now you size the trade off that distance.
questions.lesson_line: Stop first, a few cents under the low of the day. Then size it.

wrong.Right on 143.91: Right on the low, a wick that just tests it shakes you out. Give it a few cents.
wrong.A flat 3% under your fill: A percent isn't a level. The chart tells you where you're wrong, and that's the low of the day.
wrong.Halfway between fill and low: That's a stop pulled in to fit more shares. It sits inside the range, where normal noise takes you out.

questions.simple: A few cents under the low of the day, 143.91. Then you size the trade off that stop.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A3, F62)

questions.story: A leader on your list trades through its 30-minute high at 10:00. You're filled at 146.91. The low of the day so far is 143.91.

questions.q: You missed the 10:00 break and it's still going. How far over the range high can you still buy it?
questions.sentence: You can still buy up to ___% over the 30-minute high. Past that, you wait.
questions.why: 4%. Past 4% over the range high you're chasing, and chasing costs you size. Your stop stays a few cents under the low of the day. So every cent you pay up makes the stop wider and the share count smaller. If you missed it, wait for a pullback to the range high that holds. A retest or an undercut and hold of VWAP mid morning works too.
questions.lesson_line: Four percent over the range high is the line. Past it, wait for the retest.
questions.simple: 4%. Past that you're chasing, and chasing makes your stop wider and your size smaller.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (C28)

questions.q: Bysshe and Kullamagi both pick the stock off the daily chart first, then use the open only to time the buy.
questions.why: True. Bysshe builds his list from his swing setups first, then uses the opening range to time the entry. Kullamagi says you don't even need an intraday chart. Just look at the daily and buy as it starts to break out. Same idea from both of them. The daily chart is the reason to own it. The opening range just picks the moment.
questions.lesson_line: The daily chart is the reason. The opening range is the timer.
questions.simple: True, both find the setup on the daily chart. The opening range only picks the moment to buy.

reasons: the parent-setup role is a held decision (D-002); keyed only as two authors' words

questions.q: Prior close 48.10, the 200-day at 52.40. At 10:05 it breaks its 30-minute high on big volume. Can you take it?
choices: Half size with a tight stop
questions.why: No. 48.10 is under the 200-day at 52.40. For a stock that's a hard no, whatever the volume. Under the 200-day the daily trend is down, and we buy stocks that lead. One good morning on the 30-minute chart doesn't change the daily trend. Only indexes and levered ETFs get an exception, and that's a different trade.
questions.lesson_line: Under the 200-day, no long. Volume doesn't get a vote.

wrong.Yes, the volume overrides it: Nothing overrides the 200-day on a stock. A big-volume break under it is still under it.
wrong.Half size with a tight stop: Fewer shares don't fix a stock on the wrong side of the 200-day. It's still a no.
wrong.Yes, the break is clean: The 30-minute chart looks fine. The daily says the trend is down, and the daily wins.

questions.simple: No. It's under its 200-day, and that's a hard no for a stock, however big the volume.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B26)

questions.q: We only take ORBs in leaders, stocks with an RS rating of 80 or more in a strong group.
questions.why: True. The ORB is a timer, not a stock picker. RS 80 or better means the stock is already beating most of the market. Those are the names with buyers behind them when the range breaks. A clean break in a laggard is a laggard having a good morning. Check the RS Rating in our app before the open, not after the break.
questions.lesson_line: Leaders only. The break is the timer, the RS is the ticket.
questions.simple: True, we want RS 80 or better. The break is the timer and the leader is the trade.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (C31)

questions.q: Kullamagi says that on a 60-minute chart the first candle is only 30 minutes, 9:30 to 10:00.
questions.why: True. Kullamagi writes that on the 60-minute timeframe the first candle is always only 30 minutes, 9:30 to 10:00. Trade-Ideas calls the first 30-minute candle of the day the opening range. We read our range on 30-minute bars, where the first candle is 9:30 to 10:00.
questions.lesson_line: Read the range on 30-minute bars. The first candle there is 9:30 to 10:00.
questions.simple: True. Kullamagi says the first candle on a 60-minute chart is only 30 minutes long, the same half hour as our range.

questions.q: In the 10:00 bar the stock trades a cent over its 30-minute high. The bar is still open. What do you do?
choices: Put a limit order under it
questions.why: Buy it at market. The trade through the high is the trigger, so there's no close to wait for. Waiting for a bar to finish only gets you a higher price. On a strong one it's gone before you're in. A limit under the price waits for a dip that may never come. Just keep the fill within 4% of the high. This was EXEL, and the fill was 60.92.
questions.lesson_line: Set the alert at the range high. When it trades, you trade.

wrong.Wait for the 5-minute close: Our trigger is the trade through, not a close. Waiting only gets you a later, higher fill.
wrong.Wait for the 10:30 close: The range closed at 10:00. Waiting another half hour throws the entry away.
wrong.Put a limit order under it: We buy at market. A limit under the price waits for a dip that may never come.

questions.simple: Buy at market now. The trade through the high is the trigger, so you don't wait for a close.

questions.q: A $7 stock that trades $12 million a day is fine for an ORB if the range is clean.
questions.why: False. It fails both of our floors. We want $10 or more a share and at least $20 million traded a day. This one is $7 and $12 million. Thin names gap through stops and fill you badly on the way out. I don't even put stocks like that on a watchlist.
questions.lesson_line: Price and dollar volume come before the chart. $10 and $20 million a day are the floor.
questions.simple: False, we want $10 or more and at least $20 million a day. This one fails both.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B23)

questions.q: It's 9:00. Your ORB plan needs an entry, but the range won't exist until 10:00. What do you write down?
choices: A price off the premarket high
questions.why: You write the rule, not a price. Buy at market as it trades through the 30-minute high. Stop a few cents under the low of the day. Size from that distance. At 10:00 the range fills in the numbers and you're just executing. Deciding live is how you end up chasing or freezing. Entry, stop and size get written before the open, every time.

wrong.Nothing, decide live at 10:00: Deciding live is how you chase or freeze. Entry, stop and size get written before the open.
wrong.Yesterday's high as the buy: That's a different trigger, the one a Kicker can use. The ORB buys the 30-minute high.

questions.sentence: The ORB trigger stays valid for the rest of that ___.
questions.why: Session. The trigger stays valid for the rest of that session. The 30-minute window is part of the trigger's definition, not a time-of-day rule. We have no time-of-day rule. A late break is still a break.
questions.lesson_line: The range sets the level, not a deadline. The break can come any time that day.
questions.simple: The word is session. The trigger stays good all day, because the 30 minutes only define it and are not a deadline.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (C30)

questions.story: A leader on your focus list is set up for an ORB on Tuesday. It reports earnings Thursday after the close.
questions.q: Do you take Tuesday's break?
choices: Yes, it's on the focus list
questions.why: No. We don't open new buys in the 3 sessions before a report, and Tuesday is inside that window. A report can gap the stock right through your stop overnight. No stop catches that, so you could lose far more than you planned. Wait for the report. The day after is fair game, and an ORB there is a fine way in.
questions.lesson_line: Earnings is a gap your stop can't catch. Three sessions out, hands off.

wrong.Yes, it's on the focus list: The focus list doesn't override earnings. The report is the risk, and it's two days away.
wrong.Yes, at half size: Half size is still a new buy into a report. The gap doesn't care how many shares you own.
wrong.Yes, with a tighter stop: A tighter stop doesn't help. An overnight gap jumps right over it.

questions.simple: No new buys in the 3 sessions before a report. A stop can't catch an earnings gap.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B22)

questions.story: Our app's market filter reads Orange this morning: the market's under pressure, one step from Red. An A+ setup and a B setup both break their 30-minute highs at 10:00.
questions.q: Which do you take?
choices: Just the B, it's less risk
questions.why: Just the A+. In an Orange market breakouts fail more often, because the market isn't backing them. So I only want my best idea, the cleanest setup with the tightest risk. The B can wait for a better market. Green is when we press. Red is mostly cash. Orange sits in between, and that means A+ only.
questions.lesson_line: Read the market before the range. Orange buys the A+ and nothing else.

wrong.Both, full size: That's trading Orange like Green. The B waits for a better market.
wrong.Neither, Orange is cash: Red is mostly cash. Orange still lets your very best setup through.
wrong.Just the B, it's less risk: Backwards. If anything gets bought in Orange, it's the A+, the cleanest one you've got.

questions.simple: Just the A+. In Orange the market isn't backing breakouts, so only your best idea gets money.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (F65)
fixed before

questions.q: The range is 412.06 to 418.45. You fill at 418.46 and the stop goes in at 412.01. How far under your fill is the stop?
questions.why: 1.54%. 418.46 minus 412.01 is 6.45 a share. Divide 6.45 by 418.46 and you get about 1.54%. That's a tight stop, inside the 1 to 3% I like. A tight stop lets you carry real size for the same dollar risk. This was FFIV. It broke on the first bar after 10:00 and never looked back.
questions.lesson_line: Stop first, distance second, size last.
questions.simple: About 1.54%, the fill minus the stop divided by the fill. That's a nice tight stop.

reasons: computed key
3% stop width is a held decision (D-005); only A13's 'usually about 3%' is used

wrong.6.45%: 6.45 is the dollar gap, not a percent. Divide it by the fill first.
wrong.0.15%: The decimal slipped a place to the left.
wrong.15.41%: The decimal slipped a place to the right. That would be a huge stop on this chart.

questions.q: Most Kicker ORBs need a stop wider than 3.5% to work.
questions.why: False. On a Kicker the stop goes under the Kicker low, or 3.5% under your entry, whichever is closer. Most of the time you get these with a stop smaller than 3.5%. If the Kicker low is farther away than that, the cap still holds. The stop doesn't stretch to fit the trade.
questions.lesson_line: On a Kicker the stop is the Kicker low or 3.5%, whichever is closer.
questions.simple: False. The stop is capped at 3.5%, and most Kickers fit inside that with room to spare.

deeper.example: On JBI the ORB entry filled at 11.21, and 3.5% under that is 10.82, the Kicker low itself. So the cap and the low gave the same stop.

reasons: rests on the owner's 2026-11-02 Kicker ruling (v03)
fixed before (lesson line corrected)

questions.q: A Kicker ORB fills at 11.21 and you're using the 3.5% cap for the stop. Where does the stop go?
questions.why: 10.82. Multiply the fill by 0.965 to take 3.5% off: 11.21 x 0.965 is 10.82. On a Kicker the stop is the Kicker low or 3.5% under your entry, whichever is closer. On JBI the two landed in the same spot. Work the cap out before you're filled, so the stop and the size are ready the second it triggers.
questions.lesson_line: Know the cap before the fill: 3.5% under the entry, or the Kicker low if closer.
questions.simple: Take 3.5% off 11.21 and you get 10.82. Know it before the fill so you can size it.

reasons: computed key
rests on the owner's Kicker ruling (2026-11-02)

wrong.$11.60: That added 3.5%. A long's stop sits under the fill.
wrong.$7.29: Far too much off. 3.5% of 11.21 is well under a dollar.

questions.story: JBI sets up as a Kicker. It opens under the red day's high of 11.04. At 9:41 it trades through 11.04. The first 30-minute candle later tops out near 11.20.
questions.q: You planned both entries. Which one fills first?
questions.why: The prior-day-high buy. A Kicker gives you two entries, the break of the red day's high and the 30-minute ORB. When it opens under that high, the high trades first, at 9:41 here. That fill is cheaper and closer to your stop. The ORB comes after 10:00 as the confirmation. On JBI the first fill was 11.05 with a 2.3% stop. The ORB filled at 11.21, 3.7% from the same stop. That's past the 3.5% cap we use on a Kicker, so on that fill the stop comes up to 10.82.
questions.lesson_line: Opens under the red day's high: that high is your first entry. The ORB confirms it.

wrong.The ORB buy after 10:00: The ORB can't fill until the range is set. The red day's high traded at 9:41.
wrong.Nothing fills before 10:00: The prior-day-high trigger needs no range. It fires the moment 11.04 trades.
wrong.Both, size split in two: We buy full size at one price with one stop. Two entries are a choice, not a split.

questions.simple: The prior-day-high buy. It trades at 9:41, before the range is even set.

deeper.example: JBI, 2023-12-14: it opened below the red day's high. The previous-day-high entry filled at 11.05 with a stop at 10.80, 2.3% away. The ORB entry filled at 11.21, 3.7% from the same stop. At the close the first was up about 2.3R and the ORB about 1.0R.

reasons: the Kicker entry order is a proposed card line backed by the JBI example and the owner's Kicker ruling

questions.q: You can keep the ORB stop in your head until the first sell, then put it in with your broker.
questions.why: False. The stop goes in with your broker the moment you're filled. A stop in your head is a stop you argue with while the stock is falling. A real order doesn't flinch. Every position, from the first minute. And it only ever moves up.
questions.lesson_line: Real stop order with the broker, the minute you're filled.
questions.simple: False. The stop goes in with the broker right when you're filled, not later.

reasons: rests on the account rulebook D41 and A4

questions.q: You bought the 10:00 break, and by noon it's up 2R. It's still day one. What's your first sell?
choices: All of it at the close
questions.why: Nothing yet. I very rarely sell on day 1. Most of the time I wait until day 3 at the earliest. The real money comes from the 3, 5 or 7 day push, not the first morning. Sell at 2R on day one and you cap your best trades to protect a small gain. If you want protection, move the stop up to breakeven. Anywhere from 2R to 5R is fair for that.
questions.lesson_line: Day one is for holding. The first sell comes into the push.

wrong.A third now, it's up 2R: We very rarely sell on day 1. 2R is where the stop can go to breakeven, not where you sell.
wrong.A third at 3R, even today: A fixed third at 3R isn't how we sell. The first sell is a judgment into a push.
wrong.All of it at the close: That's a day trade. We swing, and the money's in the days after.

questions.simple: Nothing yet. We rarely sell on day one, and the first sell goes into a push, day 3 or later.

deeper.trap: Selling a third at 3R sounds disciplined. It caps your best trades. The first sell depends on the push. A 3, 5 or 7 day run, or about 5 to 10R, is often best.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B19, E51)
fixed before

questions.story: Your plan is a Kicker, timed with the 30-minute ORB. The red day's low is 24.10. The stock opens at 23.80.
questions.q: Is the ORB plan still on?
choices: Yes, if it gets back over 24.10
questions.why: No. A Kicker is a gap up over a red day. This one opened at 23.80, under the red day's low of 24.10. That's a gap down, the opposite of a Kicker. The ORB was only there to time the Kicker. No setup, no trade. Cross it off and go to the next name on your list.
questions.lesson_line: No setup, no ORB. The timer has nothing left to time.

wrong.Yes, wait for 10:00: The plan rode on the Kicker. Opening under the red day's low, there's no Kicker to time.
wrong.Yes, if it gets back over 24.10: A reclaim is a different trade with its own rules. This plan was the Kicker, and it's gone.
wrong.No, buy the prior-day high: That's the Kicker's other entry. No Kicker, no entry from it either.

questions.simple: No. It opened under the red day's low, so there's no Kicker, and the ORB has nothing to time.

reasons: rests on the rulebook's no setup, no trade (D44) and the card's parent-broken line (c10, a proposal)

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: After the fill, a big-volume reversal back into the range is a ___, not a second exit rule.
questions.why: A warning. After the fill the stop decides. A big-volume reversal back into the range is the classic failure shape and worth watching, but it is not a second exit rule. The stop is the exit, and it only moves up.
questions.lesson_line: Watch the reversal, honour the stop. One exit rule, not two.
questions.simple: A big-volume reversal back into the range is only a warning, because after the fill the stop is the only exit.

reasons: rests on the rulebook A4 and the card's settled line (c11)

questions.q: You're filled at 146.91 with the stop at 143.86. Where's 3R on this trade?
questions.why: 156.06. One R is your risk per share: 146.91 minus 143.86 is 3.05. Three of those is 9.15. Add 9.15 to 146.91 and 3R sits at 156.06. Mark it on your chart the minute you're filled. It's a marker, not an automatic sell. ANF got there in about three sessions, and the first sell was still a judgment call.
questions.lesson_line: Know your 3R the minute you're filled. It's a marker, not a sell order.
questions.simple: One R is 3.05 a share. Three of those on top of 146.91 puts 3R at 156.06.

reasons: computed key
rests on the owner's rulebook (B19)

wrong.$153.01: That added 3R to the stop. Start from your fill.
wrong.$137.76: That took 3R off. On a long, 3R sits above your fill.
wrong.$149.91: That added 3 dollars. One R here is 3.05, the fill minus the stop.

questions.q: The 30-minute high is 60.91. You look up at 10:20 and it's trading 63.60. How far over the high is that?
questions.why: 4.42%. 63.60 minus 60.91 is 2.69. Divide 2.69 by 60.91 and you get about 4.42%. That's past our 4% line, so you don't buy it here. Your stop is still down under the low of the day. Paying up means a wider stop and fewer shares for the same risk. Wait for a pullback to the range high that holds, or a VWAP retest.
questions.lesson_line: Measure the chase before you buy it. Past 4%, wait for the pullback.
questions.simple: 4.42% over the high. That's past our 4% line, so you pass and wait for a pullback.

reasons: computed key
rests on the owner's rulebook (C28)

wrong.104.42%: That's 63.60 divided by 60.91 with nothing taken off. The move is only the 2.69 gap.
wrong.95.77%: That's the high as a share of today's price. Measure the gap from the high.
wrong.44.16%: The decimal slipped a place to the right.

questions.story: You missed the 10:00 break. At 10:25 the stock is 6% over its 30-minute high and still climbing.
questions.q: It's still running. What's the play?
choices: Wait for a pullback that holds
Buy half size just to be in
Forget it, the trade is gone
questions.answer: Wait for a pullback that holds
questions.why: Wait for the pullback. 6% over the high is past our 4% line. Buy it there and your stop is still back under the low of the day. That's a wide stop and a small position. Size it normal and it's a big loss if it fails. I'd rather miss it than chase it. If it pulls back to the range high and holds, that's your second chance. A retest or an undercut and hold of VWAP mid morning works too.
questions.lesson_line: Past 4%, don't chase. Wait for the pullback that holds.

wrong.Buy half size just to be in: Half a chase is still a chase. Being in isn't a reason to buy.
wrong.Buy now, momentum is proof: Momentum is why it's tempting. 6% over the high is a chase, and your stop sits way down at the low.
wrong.Forget it, the trade is gone: Not gone. A pullback to the range high that holds, or a VWAP retest, gives you another shot.

questions.simple: Wait for a pullback that holds. At 6% over the high you'd be chasing with a wide stop.

deeper.trap: A stock that keeps climbing makes the chase feel safe. It isn't. Your stop stays under the low, so the distance grows and the shares shrink. Steenbarger likes the first pullback after a valid break too, once buying resumes.

reasons: rests on rulebook C28 (4%) and the owner's VWAP alternative (u01)
fixed before (a wrong choice was shortened)

questions.story: SNX: you bought the ORB at 274.04, stop 270.67. It ran past 5R, you sold some into strength and the stop went to breakeven. Then a report gaps it open under 270.67.
questions.q: What's your stop now?
choices: The low of the first 30 minutes
questions.answer: The low of the first 30 minutes
questions.why: The low of the first 30 minutes. A gap through your stop is the one time the stop rule bends. Selling the open of a gap down means selling into the panic. So you let the first half hour play out, and the low of that first 30-minute bar becomes your stop. One ceiling: if those 30 minutes take the loss past 2R, you're out. On SNX, the shares you sold into strength earlier are what kept the win.
questions.lesson_line: A gap through the stop: the first 30 minutes decide, with 2R as the ceiling.

wrong.The gap-down day's open: Selling the open sells the panic. The rule gives you the first 30 minutes.
wrong.A flat 3% under the open: A percent isn't a level. The first 30-minute low is, with 2R as the ceiling.
wrong.Breakeven, where it was: Price is already under it. The gap rule makes the first 30-minute low your stop.

questions.simple: The low of the first 30-minute bar is your new stop. If the loss goes past 2R, you're out.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B20)
fixed before

questions.q: On an ORB winner, the stop stays where you first put it until you sell the last share.
questions.why: False. The stop only moves up, and on a winner it moves. Somewhere between 2R and 5R, or at your first sell, it goes to breakeven. From there a normal pullback can't turn your winner into a loser. After that, the 9 or 20 EMA trails what's left.
questions.lesson_line: Breakeven between 2R and 5R. The stop only moves up.
questions.simple: False, once it's working the stop goes to breakeven, somewhere between 2R and 5R.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B19)
the 'first trim by default' half is the card's line
fixed before

questions.story: You got stopped out of an ORB at 10:40, your first try on this stock this week. At 11:15 it takes out the day's high.
questions.q: Can you get back in?
questions.why: Yes, as a new trade. A retake of the day's high is a fresh trigger. New fill, new stop under the low of the day, size worked out again. A stop-out isn't a verdict on the stock. Good stocks shake people out before they go. It does count as a try, though. You get 3 tries a week and 6 a month on one stock. That keeps you from revenge trading a name that isn't working.
questions.lesson_line: A stop-out isn't a verdict. The retake is a new trade, and it counts.

wrong.No, one try a day: The limit is 3 tries a week and 6 a month, not one a day.
wrong.Yes, with the old stop: New trade, new stop under its own low. The old one's done.
wrong.No, wait for tomorrow: The retake of the high is a trigger today. No reason to wait.

questions.simple: Yes. A retake of the day's high is a new trade with a new stop, and it counts as a try.

reasons: rests on rulebook B21 and E56

questions.q: A setup you like trades 3,000,000 shares a day on average. What's the most you'd ever own?
choices: No limit with a tight stop
questions.why: 30,000 shares. We never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume. 3,000,000 times 1% is 30,000. Go past that and you start to become the volume. On a bad day, getting out means pushing the price down yourself. A tight stop doesn't change that. A stop only fills if someone's there to buy from you.
questions.lesson_line: One percent of the daily volume, and not a share more.

wrong.3,000 shares: That's well under the limit. Fine to own, but it's not the most.
wrong.300,000 shares: That's ten times our limit. On a bad day you'd be most of the market.
wrong.No limit with a tight stop: A stop needs a buyer on the other side. Size past 1% and your own exit moves the price.

questions.simple: 30,000 shares, 1% of the daily volume. Past that you can't get out clean on a bad day.

reasons: computed key
rests on the owner's rulebook (D42)

questions.story: Your plan says 30-minute ORB. At 9:50 the stock is ripping, already over its 9:45 high on big volume.
questions.q: Where's your ORB trigger?
choices: Any new high on big volume
questions.why: The range high at 10:00. Until 10:00 the range isn't finished, so there's no ORB trigger yet. The 9:45 high is just a high inside the range. I get the itch too when something rips early. But your plan is the ORB, so you wait for the range and buy the trade through its high. Some strong opens can be bought right at the open. That's its own trade with its own trigger and stop, planned the night before.
questions.lesson_line: The first minutes aren't the trade. The range is, and it closes at 10:00.

wrong.Right now, over the 9:45 high: That's not your ORB. A strong open can be its own trade, but that's a different plan with a different stop.
wrong.Any new high on big volume: Volume makes it exciting, not a trigger. The trigger is the 30-minute high.
wrong.The prior day's close: The close isn't a trigger for anything here. The range high is.

questions.simple: The range high at 10:00. Before then the range isn't set, so there's no ORB trigger.

deeper.trap: The early rip is the trap. Buy at 9:50 and you have no range telling you where the real break is. Plan the trade you want to take. If you like buying strong opens, write that plan the night before.

reasons: rests on the card's named mistake (c27, a proposal)

questions.story: Same stock, same range, same volume. One day it breaks out at 10:00. Another day the break comes at 10:50.
questions.q: Is the 10:50 break still a buy?
questions.why: Yes. We have no time-of-day rule. The 30 minutes set the range. After that, a trade through the high is a trigger whenever it comes that day. QLYS broke at 10:50 and hit 5R in three sessions. Late doesn't mean weak. Plenty of good names spend the morning building and break later.
questions.lesson_line: A late break is still a break. The clock sets the range, not a deadline.

wrong.No, it's too late: There's no deadline. The range closed at 10:00 and the trigger lasts all session.
wrong.Only before 10:30: We have no time-of-day rule. A 10:30 cut-off is made up.
wrong.Yes, but at half size: Size comes from the stop and the grade, not the clock.

questions.simple: Yes. The range sets the trigger, and the trigger is good all session long.

deeper.counter: A late trigger is valid, not a promise. QLYS broke at 10:50, reached 5R in three sessions, then fell all the way back to the stop by session 10. Selling some into the push and moving the stop to breakeven is how a run like that is kept.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (C30)
fixed before

questions.story: A leader sits above its 200-day but under its 50-day after a six-week slide. It breaks its 30-minute high at 10:05 on 2x opening volume.
questions.q: Take it as an ORB on our card?
choices: Take it, but with a wider stop
questions.why: Pass. Our card wants the prior close above the 50-day simple moving average, as well as above the 200-day. This leader is above its 200-day but under its 50-day. Bysshe likewise asks for a positive daily trend, with rising 20 and 50-day averages.
questions.lesson_line: Above the 200 is the floor. Above the 50 is the trend. The ORB wants both.

wrong.Take it; the 200-day is enough: The 200-day is the hard floor. The card adds the 50-day for the trend, and this stock fails it.
wrong.Take it; the 2x volume decides: Volume does not fix a stock under its 50-day.
wrong.Take it, but with a wider stop: The stop sits a few cents under the day's low and only moves up, never wider. A wider stop does not fix a failed line.

questions.simple: Pass, because our card also wants the stock above its 50-day, and this one is under it.

reasons: the 50-day line is the card's proposed criterion, not the rulebook's
fixed before

questions.q: You've sold part of an ORB winner into a push, and the rest is riding. What takes you out of the rest?
choices: A close under the 9 or 20 EMA
questions.answer: A close under the 9 or 20 EMA
questions.why: A close under the 9 or 20 EMA. The 9 for a fast mover, the 20 for a steadier one. The rising average rides the trend with you. When price closes under it, the trend has changed and you're out. Wait for the close, not an intraday touch. Touches shake you out of good trends all the time.
questions.lesson_line: Trail the rising average. Sell the close below it, not the touch.

wrong.A touch of the 30-minute low: That was day one's stop. By now the stop sits at breakeven or higher.
wrong.The next earnings report: A report is its own call. You hold through one only if you're up 5R.
wrong.A fixed 10R target: We don't cap a winner at a number. The trail lets the big ones run.

questions.simple: A close under the 9 or 20 EMA. The close counts, not an intraday touch.

reasons: rests on rulebook E52 and E51 (E51 is marked adjustable)

questions.q: An ORB trade that's still under 1R after ten trading days gets another month to work.
questions.why: False. Ten trading days and still under 1R, you sell it. A good break should move. If it's gone nowhere for two weeks, your money's stuck while other leaders break out. Free it up for the next one.
questions.lesson_line: Ten days and nothing. The money has somewhere better to be.
questions.simple: False, still under 1R after ten trading days means you sell. The money has a better place to be.

reasons: one cited fact only (C33)
rests on the owner's rulebook (C33)

questions.story: You bought an ORB on Monday and it closed at 2.7R. Tuesday it gaps open to 3.5R.
questions.q: Up 3.5R at Tuesday's open, day 2 of the trade. What do you do?
choices: Wait for a dip, then sell
Sell it all at the close
questions.why: Hold. It's only day 2, and I very rarely sell that early. Most of the time I wait until day 3 at the earliest. Being past 3R isn't a sell signal. 3R is a marker, not an order. The first sell goes into a 3, 5 or 7 day push, often around 5 to 10R. Some days I'll sell a piece into a big gap, but that's a judgment call, never a rule. A normal day 2 gap like this, let it work.
questions.lesson_line: A gap past 3R on day 2 isn't an automatic sell. Judge the push.

wrong.Sell it all at the close: Selling everything on day 2 throws away the push you bought it for.
wrong.Sell some, it's past 3R: 3R is a marker, not a sell order. The first sell is a judgment into a push.
wrong.Wait for a dip, then sell: You sell into strength, not into a dip.

questions.simple: Hold. It's only day 2, and the first sell waits for a push of 3, 5 or 7 days.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (F63)
fixed before

questions.story: You're filled on the 10:00 break and it's working. Tonight you're writing your exit plan.
questions.q: What's the first sell going to look like?
choices: All of it at twice the range
Flat at the close of day one
A third at 3R, whatever the day
questions.why: Into a 3, 5 or 7 day push. That's when I like to sell some, often around 5 to 10R. You're selling into strength, while buyers are paying up. The rest rides the trail under the 9 or 20 EMA. Twice the range is a target from someone else's playbook. Out at the close is a day trade. And a fixed third at 3R isn't how we sell either.
questions.lesson_line: Same trigger, different trade. Our first sell goes into the push, then the trail.

wrong.A third at 3R, whatever the day: A fixed third at 3R isn't how we sell. The first sell is a judgment.
wrong.All of it at twice the range: A target of twice the range isn't our exit. It caps the big winners.
wrong.Flat at the close of day one: That's Crabel's style, a day trade. We swing, and the money's in the days after.

questions.simple: Into a 3, 5 or 7 day push, often around 5 to 10R. The rest rides the trail.

reasons: rests on rulebook B19 and E51; the others' exits are cited as theirs

questions.q: What kind of day before the open makes you like an ORB more?
choices: A climax day on huge volume
questions.why: A quiet, tight inside day. A stock that rests and gets tight the day before is coiled up. The sellers went quiet and the range shrank. When it breaks the opening range the next morning, there's room to run. An inside day or a tight base both count. It's a plus I like to see, not a must, and you judge it by eye on the daily chart.
questions.lesson_line: Quiet before the open, loud after it.

wrong.A wide-range expansion day: That's the opposite. The stock already spent its move yesterday.
wrong.A climax day on huge volume: A climax is a big move on big volume. Tight and quiet is what we want before the break.
wrong.A normal day, no pattern: Nothing wrong with it, but nothing to like either. Tight is the plus.

questions.simple: A quiet, tight day before. Tight then loose is the pattern we want.

reasons: the cue is the card's proposal and the rulebook says grading is discretionary (E50)
Crabel's line is a hypothesis from a publisher's abstract
fixed before

deeper.counter: Crabel's hypothesis was that inside days come before trend days and successful opening range breakouts. He measured quiet days as NR4 and NR7 days. We read tight by eye on the daily chart, as a plus, not a must.

questions.q: Your account is 100,000 and you're risking 0.25% on this one. Fill 274.04, stop 270.67. How many shares?
questions.why: 74 shares. 0.25% of 100,000 is $250 at risk. 274.04 minus 270.67 is 3.37 a share. 250 divided by 3.37 is 74.18, so you round down to 74. Always round down. Round up and you're risking more than you planned. The 40% position cap doesn't come into it here. The stop sets the size.
questions.lesson_line: The stop sets the size, never the other way around.
questions.simple: 74 shares. 250 dollars at risk divided by 3.37 a share, rounded down.

deeper.trap: The cap can bind. Risk a larger percent on the same trade and the risk-based size can pass the position cap of 40% of the account. The size is then the smaller of the two.

reasons: computed key
rests on the owner's rulebook (A5, A7)
changed 2026-11-10 (risk 1% to 0.25%)

wrong.296 shares: That's four times too many. Use the 0.25% you were given.
wrong.145 shares: That's about what the 40% cap would allow. The risk gives you fewer, and the smaller number wins.
wrong.7,418 shares: The 0.25% never got turned into a decimal. The risk is $250, not thousands.

questions.story: GKOS at 10:00: RS 92, 2.7x opening volume, a range 4.55% wide. The break fills at 185.11. A few cents under the low is 176.63, 4.58% away.
questions.q: What's the play?
choices: Buy it, size to the real stop
Buy, pull the stop up to 3%
Pass, the volume is too heavy
questions.answer: Buy it, size to the real stop
questions.why: Buy it, and let the real stop set the size. 4.58% is wider than I like, but under 5% I'll take it. I prefer 1 to 3%, and 3.5% is good. Past 5% I'd mostly wait for a tighter trigger. What you never do is pull the stop up to 3% to fit more shares. Then it sits inside the range, and normal noise takes you out. This one reached 0.33R and stopped out. That's fine. A loss at the stop is the plan working.
questions.lesson_line: You never pick a size and back-fit a stop inside the noise.

wrong.Pass, anything past 3% is out: 3% is the tight end of what we like, not a line. Up to 5% is fine, and this is 4.58%.
wrong.Buy, pull the stop up to 3%: That stop sits inside the range, above the real low. Noise takes you out of a good trade.
wrong.Pass, the volume is too heavy: Heavy opening volume raises the grade. It's a plus, not a warning.

questions.simple: Buy it with fewer shares. 4.58% is under the 5% we accept, so the real stop stays put.

reasons: rests on rulebook A3 and A13 (h04), with the stop-width decision (D-005) still pending
the 4.58% comes from one dossier scan row

questions.story: You bought the 10:00 break at 46.37, stop 45.51. By 10:30 it's back inside the range and under VWAP. It's still above your stop.
questions.q: How do you handle it?
choices: Hold, the stop is the exit
Hold, but sell at the close
questions.answer: Hold, the stop is the exit
questions.why: Hold. The stop decides, not your nerves. A break that falls back into the range is a warning, and I'd watch it closely. But it's not a second exit rule. Sell every fade and you'll sell the good ones that shake out and then go. This one, APA, did take the stop at 12:45. 46.37 down to 45.51 was a 1R loss, exactly the risk you planned.
questions.lesson_line: The warning tells you to watch. The stop tells you when to leave.

wrong.Sell now, it's failing: A fade is a warning, not an exit. The stop's in with the broker and it does the job.
wrong.Lower the stop for room: The stop only moves up. Never lower it.
wrong.Hold, but sell at the close: There's no exit at the close. The stop or the trail takes you out.

questions.simple: Hold. A fade back into the range is a warning to watch, and the stop is still the exit.

deeper.example: APA, 2026-09-14: a 2.3% gap above the prior day's high on 1.7x opening volume, RS 90. The break ran 0.26R, fell back through the range high by 10:30, lost VWAP and took the stop at 12:45. The loss stayed at 1R because the stop sat under the day's low.

reasons: rests on rulebook A4 and the card's settled line (c11)

questions.story: OVV: you bought the 10:30 break at 64.43, stop 63.21. It hits 5R in session 7. You sell nothing, and by session 18 it's back at 63.21.
questions.q: What would have saved the gain?
choices: A tighter stop at the low
questions.why: Selling some into the push. 5R by session 7 is exactly the push you sell into. That's the 5 to 10R zone where a first sell is often best. Sell a piece there and raise the stop to breakeven. Then the slide back takes the rest out flat, and you've banked a real win. A stop protects you from a loss. Only a sell locks in a gain.
questions.lesson_line: Sell into strength. What you sold is what you keep when the move gives it back.

wrong.A tighter stop at the low: A stop only limits losses. It can't bank a gain.
wrong.Adding shares at 5R: Adding banks nothing. More shares just means a bigger give-back.
wrong.Holding out for 10R: OVV topped at 7.53R. Waiting for 10R sold nothing.

questions.simple: Sell some into the push near 5R. A stop limits a loss, but only a sell banks a gain.

reasons: rests on rulebook B19 and E51 (the 5R step is adjustable)
the session counts come from one dossier scan row

questions.q: When an ORB triggers, you buy with a market order, not a limit.
questions.why: True. All our entries are market orders. When price trades through the range high, you hit it at market and you're in. A limit can leave you watching a good break run without you. Then the stop order goes straight in with your broker.
questions.lesson_line: Market order through the high. Stop order with the broker.
questions.simple: True, we buy at market when it trades through the high. Then the stop goes in.

reasons: rests on rulebook E57; a buy-stop (D-038, pending) would not change this answer

questions.story: A clean 10:00 break on 2.1x opening volume. The range high is over the prior day's high, and no report is near. The RS rating is 64.
questions.q: Can you take it?
choices: Pass for now, buy the retest
Take it, the break is clean
Take it, the volume says go
questions.why: Pass. We buy leaders, RS 80 or better in a strong group, and 64 isn't close. A clean break in a laggard is a laggard having a good morning. This was DHR. It got to 0.58R and stopped out. The chart looked fine. The stock just wasn't one of the strong ones.
questions.lesson_line: A clean break in a laggard is a laggard having a good morning.

wrong.Pass for now, buy the retest: A retest changes the price, not the RS. It's still a laggard.
wrong.Take it, the break is clean: The chart is one test. Leadership is another, and 64 fails it.
wrong.Take it, the volume says go: Volume raises the grade of a leader. It doesn't turn a laggard into one.

questions.simple: Pass. RS 64 is well under our 80, and a clean break doesn't make a laggard a leader.

reasons: rests on rulebook C31; the RS in the example is a proxy rank

questions.story: A leader pulls back to its 20 EMA. On the 30-minute chart, four red candles, then a green one at 11:00. The buy is over that green candle's high, well under the morning high.
questions.q: Which setup is this?
choices: A retest of the range high
questions.why: A 30-minute pivot. You're buying the first green candle after a run of red ones, right at a daily level, the 20 EMA here. The ORB buys the first half hour's high after 10:00. This buy sits well under the morning high, at a turn. Same chart, different level. Know which one you're trading, because the stop and the plan change with it.
questions.lesson_line: Find the level being bought. The range high is the ORB. The turn candle's high is the pivot.

wrong.An ORB, the 10:00 break: The ORB buys the first half hour's high. This buy sits well under it, at a turn candle.
wrong.A retest of the range high: A retest buys the pullback to the range high after a break. This buy sits well under the morning high.
wrong.An opening drive: A drive gets bought over the first bar's high in the opening minutes. This one's an 11:00 turn after a pullback.

questions.simple: A 30-minute pivot. It buys the turn candle at the 20 EMA, well under the morning high.

deeper.trap: The tell is the level and the clock. The ORB buys the first half hour's high after 10:00. The pivot buys a turn candle's high at a daily level, here the 20 EMA, often well under the morning high.

reasons: one cited fact only defines the pivot (c19)
the lookalike tells are the card's proposals, not owner rulings

questions.story: A stock gaps up 2% and runs from the bell. At 9:36 the buy fires over the first 5-minute bar's high. The day's low is inside that bar.
questions.q: What kind of entry is that?
questions.why: An opening drive. It made its low in the first 5-minute bar and got bought over that bar's high at 9:36. That's the fast version. The ORB waits for the full 30 minutes and buys after 10:00. Different clock, different stop, different plan.
questions.lesson_line: Before 10:00 there's no range to break. A 9:36 buy is the drive, not the ORB.

wrong.A 30-minute ORB: The range doesn't exist until 10:00. A 9:36 buy is the drive, the fast version.
wrong.A 30-minute pivot: A pivot needs a run of red candles into a level first. This went straight up from the bell.
wrong.A VWAP retest buy: A VWAP retest is a mid-morning buy after a dip. This went straight up from the bell, no dip.

questions.simple: An opening drive. It was bought over the first 5-minute bar at 9:36, before any 30-minute range existed.

deeper.trap: The clock is the tell. Before 10:00 no 30-minute range exists, so a 9:36 buy can't be our ORB, however strong the stock. The drive trades the first 5-minute bar. The ORB waits for the full range.

reasons: one cited fact only defines the drive (c20)
the lookalike tells are the card's proposals, not owner rulings

questions.story: A stock gaps up 3% and breaks its 30-minute high at 10:00. The day before the gap was a doji, not a red day.
questions.q: What are you looking at?
questions.why: A plain gap ORB. A Kicker needs a real red day before the gap, one that looks like a breakdown and traps sellers. A doji is just indecision. And an EP is a big gap on real news, 10% or more. A 3% gap is neither. You can still trade the break. Just grade it for what it is.
questions.lesson_line: Look at yesterday. A doji isn't a red day, so there's no Kicker.

wrong.A Kicker ORB: A Kicker needs a real red day before the gap. A doji is indecision, not a trap.
wrong.An EP: An EP is a big gap on real news. 3% isn't that.
wrong.An opening drive: A drive gets bought over the first 5-minute bar by about 9:40. This broke the 30-minute high at 10:00.

questions.simple: A plain gap ORB. A Kicker needs a real red day first, and a doji isn't one.

deeper.trap: Two checks: the day before, and the size of the gap. A Kicker needs a real red day first. A doji or a green day makes a plain gap ORB. An EP needs a big gap on a named catalyst. A 3% gap after a doji is neither.

reasons: rests on the card's lookalike rows (c21, c22), proposals and not rulings
the card's 'not traded alone' line (c28, D-002) is no longer keyed

questions.story: A stock gaps 12% on earnings. The first 30-minute range runs 7% from low to high. At 10:10 it trades through the high.
questions.q: What's your move at 10:10?
choices: Buy the break at full size
Buy, pull the stop up to 3%
questions.why: Wait for a tighter trigger. With a 7% range, your stop under the low of the day sits past 5% from the fill. That's too wide for us. I like 1 to 3%, and 5% is the most I'll take. Don't fix it by pulling the stop up into the range. Keep it on your list. A morning flush that curls back up, or a tight setup in the days after, can give you a stop that fits.
questions.lesson_line: Measure the gap and the range. A 7% range makes the stop too wide.

wrong.Buy the break at full size: Full size with a 7% range under you is a big loss if it fails. The stop's too wide.
wrong.Buy, pull the stop up to 3%: That stop sits inside the range, not under the low. Noise takes you out.
wrong.Write it off for good: A big earnings gap can give a second, tighter entry. Keep it on the list.

questions.simple: Wait. With a 7% range the stop is past 5%, so keep it on the list for a tighter entry.

deeper.trap: Don't shrink the stop to make the trade fit. The stop sits a few cents under the low of the day. We prefer 1 to 3% and accept up to 5%. Past 5%, we mostly wait for a tighter trigger.

reasons: the key rests on one card line (c22)
stop width is a held decision (D-005)
fixed before

questions.story: Two 10:00 breaks in leaders, both with the range high over yesterday's high. One came on opening volume about normal, 1.03x. The other came on 2.67x.
questions.q: Which one do you like more?
choices: No difference, a break is a break
questions.why: The 2.67x break. Heavy volume in the first half hour means the crowd showed up. Real buyers, real interest. That raises the grade. It's not a must, and a quiet break can still work. But when I'm picking, I want the one people care about. FFIV broke on 2.67x and ran 10.05R. IQV broke on 1.03x and stopped out after 1.29R.
questions.lesson_line: Heavy opening volume is the crowd showing up. It raises the grade.

wrong.The 1.03x break: Quiet is good the day before. On the break itself you want the crowd.
wrong.No difference, a break is a break: Both trigger. Volume is what grades them.
wrong.Neither, wait for a retest: The trigger is the trade through the high. A retest is only the second chance.

questions.simple: The 2.67x break. Heavy opening volume raises the grade, though it's not a must.

deeper.example: IQV: a quiet break at 10:00 with no opening interest behind it, opening volume 1.03x its 20-day mean. It reached 1.29R and stopped out. FFIV broke on 2.67x opening volume and ran 10.05R. Bysshe calls volume the best clue in the opening range.

reasons: the volume line (D-006) is pending and never keyed
the cue is the card's proposal and E50 says grading is discretionary

questions.story: 10:15, and our market reading is Green. The indexes are taking out their own opening ranges on buying. Three of your best setups sit right at their range highs.
questions.q: What's that telling you?
questions.why: Go. When the indexes take out their opening ranges on real buying, the market is backing breakouts that morning. That's when I want to execute my focus list. The index is the cue, though, not the trade. Each name still buys on its own trade through its own range high, with its own stop.
questions.lesson_line: When the indexes clear their ranges, the focus list gets the green light.

wrong.Buy the index instead: The index is the cue. Your leaders are the trades.
wrong.Wait for the close: The cue is now. Waiting for the close skips every trigger.
wrong.Nothing, indexes don't matter: They matter a lot. A break with the market behind it has a much better shot.

questions.simple: Go. The indexes clearing their ranges is the cue to work your list, one trigger at a time.

deeper.trap: A cue isn't a trigger. The indexes clearing their ranges says the list can go. Each name still needs its own trade through its range high, with its own stop.

reasons: the index cue is a proposed card line plus the owner's published note
fixed before

questions.q: EXEL: bought at 60.92, stop 59.51. It trades up to 67.97. How many R are you up?
questions.why: 5R. Your risk is 60.92 minus 59.51, which is 1.41 a share. The gain is 67.97 minus 60.92, which is 7.05. Divide 7.05 by 1.41 and you get 5. That's the low end of the 5 to 10R zone where a first sell is often best. Count in R, not dollars. R tells you how the trade is doing against what you risked.
questions.lesson_line: Count in R, not dollars. About 5R to 10R is where the first sell is often best.
questions.simple: 5R. A gain of 7.05 on a risk of 1.41 a share is five times what you risked.

deeper.example: EXEL went on to 9.06R in the sessions after. 3R on the same trade is just the fill plus three times the risk per share. It's a marker. The first sell is a judgment, often into a push of 3, 5 or 7 days.

reasons: computed key
rests on the owner's rulebook (E51)

wrong.6.0R: That measured the gain from the stop. Start from your fill.
wrong.0.2R: That's upside down. Gain over risk, not risk over gain.

questions.story: Our market reading is Red, the weakest it gets. A leader on your list breaks its 30-minute high at 10:00 on three times normal volume.
questions.q: Is this one you take?
choices: Buy it, the volume says go
Buy it and add if it works
questions.why: Pass. In a Red market I'm mostly in cash. It's a guide, not a law, but the reason is simple. When the market's falling, breakouts fail more often because there's no money chasing them. One strong break doesn't change the market. The best-looking break in a Red market is exactly what tests your discipline. Keep it on your list for when the reading turns.
questions.lesson_line: The market reading comes before the range. Red means sit on your hands.

wrong.Buy it, A+ works anywhere: Orange is the A+ only market. Red is mostly cash.
wrong.Buy it, the volume says go: Volume grades the stock, not the market. The reading still says Red.
wrong.Buy it and add if it works: Red is mostly cash. And an add is never the plan going in.

questions.simple: Pass. Red is mostly cash, so keep the name on your list for when the market turns.

deeper.trap: The best-looking break in a Red market is the test. Three times normal volume makes it tempting. Red still means mostly cash.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (F65, D46)
fixed before

questions.story: Your ORB long is up 2.2R. The company reports tomorrow before the open.
questions.q: Do you hold it through the report?
questions.why: No. You hold through a report only if you're up 5R, and this is 2.2R. A report can gap the stock right through your stop overnight. With 2.2R of cushion, one bad gap can wipe out the gain and then some. At 5R you've got room to take the hit. SNX's report on 2026-09-24 gapped it straight through the stop.
questions.lesson_line: Earnings is a gap you can't stop. 5R buys the ticket. 2.2R doesn't.

wrong.Yes, after selling half: Half is still exposed to the gap, and 2.2R is under the line.
wrong.Yes, stop at breakeven: A stop can't catch an overnight gap. Breakeven won't fill at breakeven.
wrong.Yes, 2.2R is enough cushion: The line is 5R. A report gap can be bigger than 2.2R.

questions.simple: No. We only hold through a report at 5R or more, and 2.2R isn't enough cushion for a gap.

deeper.trap: An earnings gap is the one move a stop can't cap. SNX's report of 2026-09-24 gapped it through the stop, and the shares sold into strength earlier are what kept the win. Selling half or raising the stop doesn't change the 5R line.

reasons: rests on rulebook B22 (5R)
the rule does not say whether to sell all or trim

questions.story: A Kicker with two entries. The prior-day-high buy fills at 11.05. The ORB buy fills at 11.21. Both use the same stop under the Kicker low, 10.80.
questions.q: Which fill sits closer to the stop?
questions.why: The 11.05 fill. From 11.05 the stop at 10.80 is 2.3% away. From 11.21 it's 3.7%. Same stop, higher price, more risk a share. That matters because a tighter stop buys more shares for the same dollar risk. One catch on the ORB fill: 3.7% is past our 3.5% Kicker cap, so that stop would come up to 10.82. At the close the first fill was up about 2.3R, the ORB about 1.0R. Waiting for confirmation costs you distance. Sometimes that's worth paying, sometimes not.
questions.lesson_line: Same stop, two entries. The earlier one is tighter, so it can carry more shares.

wrong.The 11.21 fill: That one's farther, 3.7% against 2.3%. Confirmation costs distance.
wrong.Same, it's the same stop: Same stop, different fills. The higher fill has the wider stop.
wrong.The 11.21, it has more room: More room means farther from the stop, not closer.

questions.simple: The 11.05 fill. Same stop, lower price, so the stop is tighter and you can own more shares.

deeper.counter: Confirmation costs distance. The ORB entry waits for the range to be proven and fills at 11.21 instead of 11.05. So the same stop sits farther away: 3.7% against 2.3%. The first entry earned about 2.3R to the ORB's 1.0R. One example, not a promise that the earlier entry always wins.

reasons: one cited example row (c07) carries the numbers
the 3.7% to the stop sits above the 3.5% Kicker cap; the owner flag asks whether the cap counts the few-cents buffer
rests on the owner's Kicker ruling

questions.q: Our rulebook has no time-of-day rule; the 30 minutes on an ORB define the trigger, not a cut-off for taking it.
questions.why: True. No time-of-day rule. The 30-minute window is part of the trigger's definition; the trigger stays valid for the rest of that session.
questions.lesson_line: The clock builds the range. It does not close the trade.

questions.story: The 30-minute low is 412.06 and the break fills at 418.46.
questions.q: Where exactly is the stop?
questions.why: A few cents under 412.06, not exactly on it. FFIV's stop was 412.01, 1.54% under the fill: the day's low at the fill, with a little room for a tick.
questions.lesson_line: Under the low, not on it. A stop on the exact low gets ticked.

wrong.Exactly 412.06: The stop sits a few cents under the day's low, not exactly on it.
wrong.A flat 3% under the fill: A percent is not a level. 3% is where the honest stop usually lands, not where it is set.
wrong.Under the prior day's low: Too far on a first break. The range low is the honest level.

questions.story: Two ranges at 10:00. In one, the high got tested twice and price sat just under it. In the other, no high repeats and the bars swing both ways.
questions.q: Which range would you rather trade?
choices: The second, more room to run
Either, a high is a high
questions.why: The first. That high got tested and price sat tight right under it. That's a real level. You know exactly where the sellers sit, and when price trades through, they're used up. The sloppy one has no level to buy and no clean low for a stop. If you can't draw the range, don't trade it.
questions.lesson_line: A range you can draw is a range you can trade. Sloppy means no level.

wrong.The second, more room to run: No clean high means no clean trigger. Room doesn't help if you can't find the entry.
wrong.Either, a high is a high: A tested high is a level. A random high is noise.
wrong.Neither, skip both: The first one is exactly what you want. Skip only the sloppy one.

questions.simple: The first. A clean high gives you a real level to buy and a clean low for the stop.

deeper.trap: Sloppy can look like energy, bars all over the place. But a trigger needs a level and a stop needs a low. Bysshe: if there isn't any well-defined support or resistance, don't waste your time watching it. OVV is the clean case: a tight hold just under the range high, then a trigger at 10:30.

reasons: the cue is the card's proposal and E50 says grading is discretionary

questions.story: A leader, RS 81, over its 50 and 200-day, opens flat on 2.67x volume. The first 30-minute candle runs 412.06 to 418.45.
questions.q: Write the plan: entry, stop, first sell.
questions.why: Market at 418.46, stop 412.01, and a judged first sell. You buy at market the moment it trades through 418.45. The stop goes a few cents under the 412.06 low, not right on it. The first sell is a judgment into a push, not a fixed third at 3R. This was FFIV. It broke on the first bar after 10:00 and ran to 10.05R.
questions.lesson_line: Entry, stop, first sell, trail. Write the rule before the open.

wrong.Market 418.46, stop 412.01, third at 3R: A fixed third at 3R isn't how we sell. The first sell is a judgment.
wrong.Market 418.46, stop 412.06, judged sell: That's right on the low. The stop goes a few cents under it.
wrong.Limit 418.46, stop 412.01, judged sell: We buy at market. A limit can leave you watching it go.

questions.simple: Buy at market through the high, stop a few cents under the low, and judge the first sell.

deeper.example: FFIV, 2026-09-15: the rule written before the open gave, at 10:00, a buy at 418.46 and a stop of 412.01. That's a few cents under the 412.06 low and 1.54% under the fill. It broke on the first bar after 10:00 and ran to 10.05R in the sessions after.

reasons: rests on rulebook E57, F62 and B19
a buy-stop (D-038) would not change this key
numbers come from one dossier scan row

questions.story: You bought at 60.92, stop 59.51, so 2R under your entry is 58.10. Next week it gaps open at 58.90. The first 30-minute low prints 57.20.
questions.q: Where does that leave you?
choices: Hold and wait for the close
questions.why: Out. On a gap through your stop, the first 30-minute low becomes the new stop, but only up to 2R. One R is 60.92 minus 59.51, so 2R under your entry is 58.10. The first 30 minutes printed 57.20, under that line. The rule gives you the half hour, not a blank cheque. Past 2R, you take the loss and move on.
questions.lesson_line: The gap rule gives you the first 30 minutes, not a blank cheque. Past 2R, you're out.

wrong.Sell at the open, 58.90: The open is still inside 2R. The rule gives you the first 30 minutes.
wrong.Stop moves to 57.20: Only inside 2R. 57.20 is past the 58.10 line.
wrong.Hold and wait for the close: There's no close rule here. Past 2R, you're out.

questions.simple: Out. The first 30 minutes took the loss past 2R, so the 30-minute low doesn't become your stop.

deeper.trap: The trap is taking the new stop without checking the ceiling. The gap opened at 58.90, still above the 2R line at 58.10, so the open alone doesn't force you out. The first 30 minutes printed 57.20, under it. That's what takes you out.

reasons: rests on rulebook B20 and its 2R ceiling
a computed key (2R level)

questions.story: Same stock, same week. You got stopped out Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday, one try each day. Thursday morning a new break prints.
questions.q: Do you take Thursday's break?
choices: No, the cap is 2 a week
questions.why: No. One stock gets 3 tries a week and 6 a month. Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday used all three. Every new trigger is a new trade, and that's exactly why each one counts. Three stops in a row is the stock telling you it isn't ready. Let it go, and come back next week if it sets up again.
questions.lesson_line: Three tries a week, six a month. A fourth this week is a pass.

wrong.Yes, new trigger, new trade: It's a new trade, and that's why it counts. The cap is 3 a week.
wrong.Yes, at half size: Size doesn't reset the count. Three is three.
wrong.No, the cap is 2 a week: Right answer, wrong reason. The cap is 3 tries a week and 6 a month.

questions.simple: No, you get three tries a week on one stock and you've used them. Come back next week.

deeper.trap: 'A new trigger is a new trade' is true, and that's why the count matters. Each try had its own stop, and each one counted. Three a week on one stock is the weekly cap. Six in a month is the monthly cap.

reasons: rests on rulebook E56 and B21; a week is not defined in the rulebook

questions.story: A leader reported last night and gaps 3% this morning on heavy volume. At 10:05 it trades through its 30-minute high.
questions.q: Is the break buyable?
choices: Yes, the report is behind it
questions.answer: Yes, the report is behind it
questions.why: Yes. The blackout is the 3 sessions before a report. This one already reported, so the gap risk you were avoiding is gone. The news is out, and the market voted with a gap up on heavy volume. That's a fine place for an ORB. Same plan as always: buy the trade through the high, stop under the low of the day.
questions.lesson_line: The blackout is before the report, not after it.

wrong.Yes, but only after 11:00: We have no time-of-day rule. A trade through the high is the trigger all session.
wrong.No, too close to earnings: Close isn't the rule. Before is. The report's done.
wrong.No, wait three sessions: The 3 sessions sit before the report, not after it.

questions.simple: Yes, we avoid the 3 sessions before a report, not after. This one already reported.

deeper.example: TMDX, APPS and GRRR are ORBs taken the day after a report. The blackout only covers the 3 sessions before one.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B22)
fixed before

questions.q: Kullamagi sells a third to a half after 3 to 5 days. Our rule sells a third at 3R and a third at 5R.
questions.why: True. Kullamagi: sell a third to a half after 3 to 5 days, then move the stop to breakeven. Ours sells by R: a third at 3R, another at 5R, then the trail.
questions.lesson_line: His clock, our ladder. Same stop, different exit.

questions.story: You bought the ORB at the size your plan set. An hour later it runs through the next daily level and keeps going.
questions.q: Do you add as it clears the level?
choices: Not as a plan. One buy, one stop
Yes, a third more, same stop
questions.answer: Not as a plan. One buy, one stop

Add higher and your average price rises, so a normal pullback now costs more than you planned. Adding to a working winner on strength does happen, but it's rare and a feel call. Strength gets paid through the sells into the push and the trail.

questions.story: Two 10:00 breaks. One stays above the range high for 20 minutes. The other pokes above it, drops back inside after 3 minutes, then goes above it again.
questions.q: Which break do you trust more?
questions.why: The one that held. Price sat over the range high for 20 minutes. Buyers took the level and kept it. The other one fell back inside after 3 minutes. Both triggered, but only one showed you the sellers were done. A drop back into the range on big volume is how these fail, so that's what I watch for.
questions.lesson_line: A good break holds above the range high. Falling back inside is the warning.

wrong.The one that broke twice: Falling back inside means it didn't hold. Breaking twice isn't strength.
wrong.Both the same: Both triggered. Only one held, and holding is what you want to see.
wrong.Neither, only a close counts: The trigger is the trade through the high, not a close. Both triggered.

questions.simple: The one that held. Holding over the range high shows the buyers took the level.

deeper.trap: The 3-minute break is still a trigger, since the first trade through the high is. What it didn't do is hold. Bysshe's rule of thumb: price holds above the range for half the range's length, about 15 minutes on a 30-minute range.

questions.story: A leader closed yesterday at 63.90. Its 20-day sits at 64.40, its 50-day at 63.30 and its 200-day at 55.60. At 10:05 it breaks its 30-minute high.
